name: Uma Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Uma, and thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. We don't sell anything or campaign. Whatever you say stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a fibre laser cutter at a sheet metal shop on the Northgate estate, about forty people, mostly making brackets, panels and enclosures for other factories. My day is loading steel sheets with the vacuum lifter, calling up the cutting program, watching the first part come off and checking it with the calipers, then sorting the cut parts onto pallets for the press brake. I've been there two years and I still mess up the nesting sometimes, which is how you lay the parts on the sheet so you don't waste metal. The bit that wears me out is the night before a big order, when the supervisor stands behind you counting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was home with the kids for a long time, then a few years on the tills at a garden centre. A friend got me an interview at the shop and I just liked it straight away, the hum of the machine and seeing a flat sheet turn into a real thing. I'm the slowest operator there but I'm the one who looks things up. I've got a chatbot on my phone that I ask about everything, from fault codes to how to talk to my son's teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit gutted, actually. Everyone else would be laughing that it was overhyped, and I'd be the one saying it's still useful for me. My partner Jonas would tease me for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay how they are, which is fine. I'd still use it to learn faster, and I'd still be pushing to get better on the machine. Nothing to fear, just nothing to get excited about either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at what I'm doing, learning to program the cutter myself instead of waiting for Kev in the office. I'd ask the boss to send me on the press brake course next year. And we'd keep our savings where they are, about three months, and maybe start a little fund for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the chatbot every day. If it's mostly hype, does that change how you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep using it the same way. It already saved me a whole sheet of stainless once, when it explained why my lead-in was too close to the edge. That's worth something even if it's not the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn next in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Programming the nests myself, then the press brake. I want to be the person who can run the whole cell, not just push the green button.

S0.say: She'd admit she's a bit gutted while everyone else laughed that it was overhyped. She'd keep saying it's still useful for her, and her partner would tease her for weeks.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, which is fine. She'd still use AI to learn faster and push to get better on the machine, with nothing to fear and nothing to get excited about.
S0.do: Keeps learning to program the cutter herself and asks for the press brake course next year. Keeps about three months of savings and maybe starts a small fund for the kids.
S0.quote: I want to be the person who can run the whole cell, not just push the green button.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is the only operator in her shop who reads up on everything, and she sees AI as a learning partner rather than a threat. A flat future disappoints her slightly but doesn't worry her. She is driven by wanting to understand the whole process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is coming whatever we do, so the question is who gets the gains. Workers should get training paid for and a say in how it's brought in. I'd say that online and at the pub, and I'd probably start a few arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could be good for me. The loading and sorting will get automated, but someone has to program it and watch it, and I'm already the one with the chatbot open. I'd be worried for the others more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the boss within a month and offer to be the person who learns the new kit. I'd do an online course in CAD drawing, the cheap one I've had bookmarked for months. And I'd talk to the guys about joining the union, because the shop isn't unionised and that would matter now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of guilt underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about who gets the gains. How do you square that with being so keen on the tech itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy. I like the tools, I don't like who owns them. A robot that does the heavy lifting is great, as long as the company doesn't keep every penny it saves and bin half the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd ask your boss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they're planning to bring in an automatic loader, and whether they'll train someone already here to run it, not hire in. And I'd say it should be me, cheekily.

S1.say: The change is coming, so the question is who gets the gains. Workers should get paid training and a say in how it's introduced, and she'd argue it online and at the pub.
S1.think: It could be good for her, because someone has to program and watch the new machines and she's already the one using AI. She worries more about her colleagues than herself.
S1.do: Asks her boss within a month to be the one trained on new kit and starts a cheap online CAD course. Talks to colleagues about unionising the shop.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some guilt underneath about colleagues.
S1.quote: I like the tools, I don't like who owns them.
S1.fieldNote: Uma combines enthusiasm for the technology with a clear politics about ownership. She plans both a personal upgrade and a union drive in a non-union shop. Her guilt about being better placed than her colleagues was the most honest moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and public ownership of some of it, because otherwise a handful of companies own everything. I'd be loud about it. I'd join whatever campaign started up, and I'd use the AI tools to help organise it, which is a bit funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my head start doesn't count for much if the machine can program itself. I'd be useful for a year, maybe, as the person who babysits it. After that, I'm a 45-year-old with a school certificate and the same as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the go-to person for the new robots in the first months, to last as long as possible. We'd save everything we could, and Jonas would need a plan too, because his delivery job would go early. I'd look for work that's about people, like the community centre, and get involved in the campaign straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Scared for Jonas more than me, oddly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. Does being an early adopter help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It buys me time, and it means I'm not frozen like some of the lads would be. But you can't outrun something that learns faster than you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's not their fault and not ours, it's a big change that happened to everyone at once. Mia's thirteen and already asks me what job she should do. I'd tell her I don't know, and that's the first time I've had no idea at all.

S2.say: This is the moment for a basic income and some public ownership, or a handful of companies own everything. She'd join a campaign and use AI tools to help organise it.
S2.think: Her head start counts for little if the machine programs itself; she'd be useful for a year at most. After that she's in her mid-forties with a school certificate like everyone else.
S2.do: Makes herself the go-to person for the new robots to last as long as possible. Saves everything she can, helps her partner plan for losing his delivery job, looks at people-centred work and joins the campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious, and oddly more scared for her partner than for herself.
S2.quote: You can't outrun something that learns faster than you do.
S2.fieldNote: Her early adoption helps her stay active rather than freeze, but she sees its limits clearly. She worries most about her partner, whose delivery job she thinks would go first. Telling her daughter she has no idea which job to pick visibly shook her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with time to build it properly. I'd want unions, councils and companies sat round the same table working out what happens to everyone. I'd probably end up running some local group about it, knowing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can actually move, not just scramble. I'd use the first two to make myself useful with the robots and the last three to get into something that lasts longer. I'm not sure what that is yet, but I'd have time to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in year one, maybe community work or teaching assistant, alongside the job. We'd save an extra hundred and fifty a month and get Jonas onto something too. I'd use the AI tools every day to learn faster, which is what they're good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like nervous before a big day than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for Jonas, mainly. He'd hate retraining, but with five years I could drag him along to a course with me. Two years and he'd just sit on the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work about people. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people want a person there. Teaching adults to use the machines, maybe, until the machines teach themselves. Or helping at Leo's school, he's got a lovely teaching assistant who's made a real difference.

S3.say: The message stays the same, but with time to build it properly, with unions, councils and companies at one table. She'd probably end up running a local group about it.
S3.think: Five years means she can move, not scramble, using the first two years to be useful with the robots and the next three to shift into longer-lasting work. She'd have time to find out what that is.
S3.do: Starts a part-time course in community work or teaching assistance in year one alongside her job. Saves an extra hundred and fifty a month, helps her partner retrain and uses AI daily to learn faster.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more like nerves before a big day than dread.
S3.quote: Two years and he'd just sit on the sofa.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her from survival mode into planning, and much of the plan is about pulling her partner along. She imagines teaching adults or supporting children as work that keeps a human in the room. She seems energised by organising other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it right, so no excuses. Shorter weeks, retraining as a right, a share for everyone. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd be at the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to change jobs properly, maybe twice. I'd be 53, and I'd hope to be doing something with people that I'd chosen. Honestly, it's the version where I might come out better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the shop and get really good on the new kit for the first few years, then train as a teaching assistant or adult tutor. I'd put a bit into an index fund, nothing fancy, because if robots make the money I'd want a tiny slice. And I'd help set up a union branch at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the mild kind. More curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, is there anything you'd hold off on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holding off on the big decisions, like moving house or picking a new career for good. In ten years the whole picture changes three times. I'd keep my options open and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the politicians to do with that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan for it, properly. Pay for retraining, protect people's homes and set up some kind of shared fund. And actually ask workers, not just companies, what they need.

S4.say: There's time to do it right, so there are no excuses: shorter weeks, retraining as a right and a share for everyone. She'd say it to anyone and be at the meetings.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to change jobs properly, maybe twice, and she'd hope to be doing chosen work with people at 53. This is the version where she might come out better.
S4.do: Stays at the shop and gets good on the new kit, then trains as a teaching assistant or adult tutor. Puts a little into an index fund and helps set up a union branch at the shop.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, more curious than worried.
S4.quote: In ten years the whole picture changes three times.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Uma sees a chance to come out ahead and plans two career moves. She'd invest a little so she owns a slice of what robots earn, which sits alongside her calls for shared funds. She deliberately holds off on big, fixed decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because being ready doesn't help if nobody else is. What would help is money for families while they find their feet, like a basic income, and free courses that start the same month, not a year later. And something for people like Jonas who won't go looking for help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd miss the work itself. I would. There's a moment when the laser pierces the sheet and it sparks like a firework, and I still watch it every time.

headlineQuote: There's a moment when the laser pierces the sheet and it sparks like a firework, and I still watch it every time.
portrait: Uma Bauer, 43, runs a fibre laser cutter at a forty-person sheet metal shop, still the slowest operator but the one who looks everything up with her phone's chatbot. She likes the tools and distrusts who owns them, pairing personal upskilling with a push to unionise. Under steady change she is excited and a little guilty about colleagues, while fast AGI makes her anxious, mostly for her delivery-driver partner. Given five or ten years she plans moves into teaching or community work and sees a chance to come out better.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because being ready on her own doesn't help when nobody else has had time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income while families find their feet, free courses starting the same month, and help that reaches people like her partner who won't look for it.
